My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

vignette: Meet Thomas, a 52-year-old married man who has been a school principal for over two decades. His life took a dramatic turn six months ago when he was assaulted by a disgruntled parent in his office. The event left him shaken, and as the days turned into weeks, Thomas found himself struggling to recall the details of that fateful day deliberately. When he tried to remember what happened, he would feel his mind fogging up, as if there was an invisible barrier preventing him from accessing those memories. Despite the difficulty in recalling the event, Thomas's memories of the assault would often replay like a film in his mind, unbidden and unwelcome. He would see himself sitting behind his desk, facing the angry parent, feeling helpless and scared. These replays were so vivid that Thomas would sometimes feel his body reenacting the same position as when the event occurred – he'd be standing in his kitchen or walking down a hallway, and suddenly his muscles would tense up, and his posture would shift, as if he was back in that moment. As these memories replayed, Thomas began to notice how they affected him in other ways. He started feeling jumpy and easily startled, even when there was no apparent reason for it. Simple noises like the school bell or a slamming door would make him jump. He also found himself scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building, his eyes instinctively searching for a way out. Thomas couldn't shake off the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. The more these memories replayed, the more vigilant Thomas became in his daily life. He started noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects in his environment – a sharp pencil on his desk, a broken chair leg in the cafeteria, or even a student's backpack with its straps and metal buckles. His mind would quickly turn these harmless objects into potential threats, making him feel like he was walking through a minefield. As the weeks went by, Thomas's behavior became more pronounced. He started avoiding certain areas of the school, fearing that they might trigger another memory replay or make him feel vulnerable. His relationships with his staff and students began to suffer as well – he became more irritable and withdrawn, always on edge. The final straw came when a student accidentally bumped into him in the hallway, causing Thomas to flinch violently and almost knock over a nearby chair. It was then that he realized he needed help to break this cycle of fear and anxiety. Now, Thomas is seeking therapy, hoping to find a way to overcome his PTSD symptoms and regain control over his life. He's most afraid of losing himself completely in these memories and threat perceptions, becoming trapped in a world where danger lurks around every corner. As he begins this journey towards healing, Thomas holds onto the hope that one day he'll be able to walk through those school hallways without feeling like he's walking on eggshells.
